emeraldMineToursColombia.metaTitle: Emerald Mine Tours in Colombia: 2026 Guide | Andean Scapes
emeraldMineToursColombia.metaDescription: How to visit a real emerald mine in Colombia: the emerald regions, getting to Chivor from Bogotá, what happens inside the mine, safety and what to bring.
emeraldMineToursColombia.title: Emerald mine tours in Colombia: a practical 2026 guide
emeraldMineToursColombia.lead: Almost every "emerald tour" at the top of Google happens in Bogotá, among jewelers and the traders of Avenida Jiménez. Going into a mine is something else: you travel to the mining regions, put on a helmet and boots, and accept that no stone may turn up. This is how it works in Chivor.
emeraldMineToursColombia.imageAlt: Visitors in helmets and boots at the entrance of an emerald mine in Chivor, Boyacá

whatIs.heading: What is an emerald mine tour?
paragraphs: It is a guided visit to a working emerald mine, alongside local miners. The mines we visit in Chivor are real emerald mines: some are worked by hand and others at a larger scale. They are not coal mines or mock-ups built for tourists. It is what many people look for as "miner for a day": a day alongside the miners, not a job.

You enter with a local guide, a helmet and boots. Time underground is only part of the day, which also includes the 4x4 ride up from town, preparation and, depending on the tour, hiking or horseback riding along the mining trails. Finding an emerald is possible but never guaranteed.

This is different from the emerald tours in Bogotá, which show the trade, cutting and jewelry in the city but never enter a mine. To see where the stone comes from, you have to travel to the mining regions.

regions.heading: Where are the emerald mines in Colombia?
paragraphs: Colombian emeralds come from two belts in the Eastern Andes. The western belt, in western Boyacá, includes Muzo, Coscuez, Maripí, Quípama, Otanche, Pauna and San Pablo de Borbur. The eastern belt includes Chivor, Somondoco, Macanal and Guateque in Boyacá, and Gachalá and Ubalá in Cundinamarca.

They are separate destinations, several hours apart by road, so they don't combine well in a short trip. Chivor is considered the source of the first emeralds that left the Americas after the Spanish conquest, and in 1967 Gachalá produced one of the world's most famous emeralds, an 858-carat crystal. By department, almost all are in Boyacá; in Cundinamarca there are mines in Gachalá and Ubalá, in the Guavio region.

chivor.heading: Why visit Chivor
paragraphs: Chivor sits at about 2,000 meters above the Sinaí valley, which further down becomes the Guavio river, with a cool climate and cold nights. From the El Púlpito viewpoint, just below the mines, you can see towards the Eastern Plains (Llanos) on clear days.

Beyond its history, which runs from the Muisca peoples to the mining engineer Peter W. Rainier and his book Green Fire, Chivor lets you enter active mines with miners from the community. Our base is Hacienda El Recuerdo in Mundo Nuevo (Ubalá), very close to Chivor, a cattle and beekeeping farm where guests stay on the two-day tours.

gettingThere.heading: How to get to Chivor, Boyacá, from Bogotá
paragraphs: From Bogotá, take the road towards Tunja; at El Sisga, turn right down into the Tenza Valley and continue to Chivor, without going on to Tunja. Near Macanal you cross the La Esmeralda reservoir by ferry during its operating hours, or drive around it. The trip takes about 5 to 6 hours, because the last stretch is an unpaved mountain road.

You can reach Chivor town by bus, car or motorbike; from there, the local 4x4 ride to the mine is included in every tour. If you would rather not drive, we offer a private round-trip 4x4 transfer from Bogotá at extra cost; the price is per vehicle and covers up to 4 people.

An alternative route via Ubalá, in the Guavio region, is only suitable for a motorbike or a 4x4: it is about 35 km of rural road to the hacienda. With a regular car, the right option is to arrive via Chivor town.

inside.heading: What happens inside the mine
paragraphs: The day starts with a talk with local miners and artisans about how emeralds are found. Then you are given safety gear and enter the tunnels with your guide, where there is water, mud and uneven ground.
Inside, you see how the miners work, how a vein is followed and which minerals come with the emerald. The two-day tours also include an emerald workshop of about an hour on how the stone is graded.

If an emerald turns up during the visit, it is agreed on the spot with the miners and the guide, who share what is found. The value of the experience lies in the emerald culture, nature and food of the region, not in the find.

choose.heading: How to choose your tour
paragraphs: The day trip includes one mine and a hike in a single day. It is doable, but it is a long day: you leave Bogotá before dawn and add another 5 to 6 hours to drive back.
The 2-day/1-night tour includes one mine, a hike, the workshop, a night at Hacienda El Recuerdo and 4 meals. The most complete tour adds a second mine and a guided horseback ride of about 2 hours.
The minimum age is 5, and dogs can join the group inside the mine in Chivor. If you have reduced mobility, a heart condition or a severe phobia, ask us before booking.

safety.heading: Safety, Chivor weather and what to bring
paragraphs: You always enter with a guide and safety gear, in mines with controlled access, and every tour includes medical assistance cover during the experience. The team checks local and mine conditions before each departure.

The dry season runs from December to February and the rainy season from May to August. Bring shoes that can get wet and muddy, a full change of clothes, a small towel, a light or waterproof jacket, water, sunscreen and cash for local expenses.

logistics.heading: This is not a trip to the Salt Cathedral
paragraphs: The Salt Cathedral of Zipaquirá is an hour from Bogotá, with parking, restaurants and buses every few minutes. An emerald mine is another matter. Chivor is about 160 to 180 km from the capital, depending on the route, which means 5 to 6 hours on the road; western Boyacá is just as far or farther. The mine entrances are not in town: you reach them on unpaved mountain tracks that a regular car will not climb.

That makes transport the hardest part of the trip. Tourism in the region is still small, there is no transfer market like in the big destinations, and what works is a 4x4 with a driver from Bogotá. That driver works a full day out and another back, and it shows in the price. Our private 4x4 transfer, round trip Bogotá–Chivor–Bogotá, costs 1,700,000 COP per vehicle and carries up to 4 people (reference price as of November 2026). For a couple on the two-day tour, at 475,000 COP per person, the transport costs more than the tour itself. You can also take a bus to Chivor town, the cheapest option, and ride up from there in our local 4x4.

The other problem is where to sleep and eat. Chivor is a small municipality with few hotels and few restaurants, and the mine is far from the town center. Arrive on your own and you have to sort out lodging, meals, transport to the mine entrance and the mine visit separately, each with a different provider and with little phone signal to coordinate them.

An all-inclusive tour settles those pieces at once: a night at Hacienda El Recuerdo, meals, local 4x4 transport and the mining day, with no middlemen between you and the people of the region. And you spend the trip with hosts and guides who live there, who can change the plan when it rains and who know what no map shows. You can put it all together yourself, of course; just expect more phone calls and more surprises.

chivorHistory.metaTitle: History of the Chivor Emerald Mine | Andean Scapes
chivorHistory.metaDescription: From Somondoco to Peter Rainier and Green Fire: the history of the Chivor emerald mines, their rediscovery in 1896 and the El Púlpito viewpoint.
chivorHistory.title: History of the Chivor emerald mine: from Somondoco to Green Fire
chivorHistory.lead: Chivor was one of the first emerald sources the conquistadors knew, lay lost under the forest for two centuries and lived a second age of adventure in the 1920s. This is its story, based on research published by the Gemological Institute of America (GIA).
chivorHistory.imageAlt: Mountains and valley of the Chivor emerald mines, Boyacá

somondoco.heading: Somondoco: emeralds before the conquest
paragraphs: When the Spanish reached the Eastern Andes, the Chibcha (Muisca) peoples were already wearing emeralds in their jewelry. The deposit we now call Chivor was known as Somondoco, after the nearby village where the stones were sorted.

According to the historians cited by GIA, emeralds from this area were traded long before the conquest, and Chivor is considered the source of the first emeralds that left the Americas for the rest of the world.

conquest.heading: 1537: Valenzuela's expedition
paragraphs: In 1537, Gonzalo Jiménez de Quesada learned of the Somondoco mines and sent captain Pedro Fernández Valenzuela to find them. Valenzuela reported that, from the heights of the mines, he could see the Orinoco plains through an opening in the range. That detail would prove decisive centuries later.

The Spanish worked Chivor through the 16th and 17th centuries with indigenous labor, devastated within a few decades. A royal decree of 1593 ordered humane treatment of the miners; in 1602 Philip III demanded it be enforced, by which time it was too late. The first recorded concession dates from 1592. In 1672 the mine was abandoned by order of the Crown, and the forest covered it for about two hundred years while attention moved to Muzo.

rediscovery.heading: 1896: Francisco Restrepo's rediscovery
paragraphs: In the late 19th century, the Colombian mining engineer Francisco Restrepo studied, in the National Library, the friars' chronicles describing the lost Somondoco mines. After some eight years of searching the range, he found the mine in 1896: the decisive clue was the view towards the plains.

From 1911 the German Fritz Klein, from Idar-Oberstein, worked there and in 1925 published the first detailed account of the mine, Smaragde unter dem Urwald (Emeralds Under the Jungle). In the early 1920s Chivor yielded the Patricia emerald, a 632-carat crystal now on display at the American Museum of Natural History in New York.

rainier.heading: Peter W. Rainier and Green Fire
paragraphs: Peter W. Rainier, a mining engineer born in southern Africa in 1890, managed Chivor from 1926 to 1931 for a New York company. On arrival he drove an iron stake into El Púlpito to mark the edge of the concession. When the board ordered him to close the loss-making mine, he kept working, and within a week the first vein appeared.

After the 1929 crash his employers closed the mine. Rainier stayed in the region and, with his wife Margaret, founded Las Cascadas, a tea plantation on the slopes of the Guavio valley about 15 km from Chivor, described as the first commercial tea plantation in South America. When he was at the mine, the couple signaled each other with flashlights every night.

In 1942 he published his memoir, Green Fire. John Sinkankas, author of the major annotated bibliography of gemology, called it "colorful, sometimes sensational", yet full of valuable detail. In 1954 MGM released a film of the same title starring Grace Kelly and Stewart Granger.

pulpito.heading: El Púlpito: the viewpoint over the plains
paragraphs: El Púlpito is a sandstone monolith hanging over the Sinaí river valley, just below the mine. Further down, the Rucio and Sinaí rivers join to form the Guavio.

From here you can see the gap in the mountains that looks out to the Eastern Plains, the same view Valenzuela described in 1537 and that guided Restrepo in 1896. In 2015 a GIA team retracing Rainier's steps found the hole left by his iron stake in the rock. The viewpoint is part of our day trip.

today.heading: Chivor today: where the mines are
paragraphs: Today mining in Chivor is mostly done in underground tunnels, in mines of different scales along the Sinaí valley. Emeralds form in veins within Cretaceous black shales, and chromium and vanadium give them the slightly bluish green that characterizes Chivor stones. The mines lie in the municipality of Chivor, in the Oriente province of Boyacá. The town is the starting point; you ride up to the mine entrances by 4x4.
Miners have their own vocabulary: chispas are small, intensely colored crystals and gotas de aceite (oil drops) are the finest. At the mine you will hear both words before you see a single stone.

gachalaGuavio.metaTitle: The Gachalá Emerald (858 Carats) and the Guavio Valley | Andean Scapes
gachalaGuavio.metaDescription: The story of the 858-carat Gachalá emerald, now at the Smithsonian, and of the Guavio valley that links Gachalá with Chivor and Hacienda El Recuerdo.
gachalaGuavio.title: The Gachalá emerald and the Guavio valley
gachalaGuavio.lead: The most famous emerald of the eastern belt is not in Colombia. It sits in a display case at the National Museum of Natural History in Washington. It came out of a Gachalá mine in 1967, in the same Guavio valley where we operate today.
gachalaGuavio.imageAlt: Rural landscape of the Guavio valley near Chivor

stone.heading: The Gachalá emerald: 858 carats
paragraphs: The Gachalá emerald was found in 1967 at the La Vega de San Juan mine, in the municipality of Gachalá (Cundinamarca). It is an 858-carat crystal, about 172 grams and roughly 5 centimeters long, of an intense green.

New York jeweler Harry Winston donated it to the Smithsonian Institution in 1969, and it is now part of the permanent collection of the National Museum of Natural History in Washington. It is named after the municipality where it was found; by tradition, Gachalá means "place of Gacha" in the Chibcha language.

belt.heading: Emerald mines in Cundinamarca: Gachalá and the eastern belt
paragraphs: Gachalá belongs to Colombia's eastern emerald belt, together with Chivor, Somondoco, Macanal, Guateque and Ubalá. It is a different belt from western Boyacá, home to Muzo and Coscuez.
In this belt, emeralds occur in veins within Cretaceous sedimentary rocks, and its mining history goes back to the Chibcha peoples who already worked the Somondoco area, now Chivor.

valley.heading: The Guavio valley
paragraphs: Below the Chivor mines, the Rucio and Sinaí rivers join to form the Guavio river. A hanging bridge over the Rucio marks the border between Cundinamarca and Boyacá, and on the valley slopes, about 15 km from Chivor, lie the ruins of Las Cascadas, the tea plantation Peter and Margaret Rainier founded in the 1930s. Downstream, the Guavio fills the reservoir of Colombia's largest operating hydropower plant, which also receives the Chivor river through a 2.2 km tunnel.

In 2015 a GIA team spent six days traveling from Gachalá to Chivor, first by 4x4 and then on foot and by mule, by way of Las Cascadas and the hamlet of Montecristo. They described a landscape of waterfalls hundreds of meters high, bromeliads and birds of prey.

hacienda.heading: Hacienda El Recuerdo: our base in the Guavio
paragraphs: Hacienda El Recuerdo is in Mundo Nuevo, in the municipality of Ubalá (Cundinamarca), within the Guavio region and very close to Chivor. It is a cattle and beekeeping farm with private rooms and WiFi, where guests on our two-day tours stay.
Tours start and end in Chivor town. From Ubalá it is about 35 km of rural road to the hacienda, a route suitable only for a motorbike or a 4x4; with a regular car, it is best to arrive via Chivor.

visit.heading: How to visit the region
paragraphs: To experience the eastern belt without planning an expedition, start in Chivor: one mine, a night at Hacienda El Recuerdo and the drive back to Bogotá through the Tenza Valley, about 5 to 6 hours.
If you also want to explore Gachalá and the Guavio valley, check road conditions first, as the roads are rural and change with the rains, and plan at least one extra day.

travelSafety.metaTitle: Is Chivor Safe to Visit? 2026 Traveler Guide | Andean Scapes
travelSafety.metaDescription: What official travel advice says about Boyacá, why Colombia's eastern emerald belt has a different history, plus roads, money, photos and emergencies in Chivor.
travelSafety.title: Is Chivor safe to visit? What to know before you travel
travelSafety.lead: It comes up in almost every conversation with travelers from outside Colombia, and it is a fair question. The short answer: Chivor is not in any area that foreign travel advisories tell you to avoid, but it is rural mountain country and you travel by a few clear rules. Here they are, with sources.
travelSafety.imageAlt: Mountain landscape in the Chivor emerald region, Boyacá

advice.heading: What official travel advice says
paragraphs: The UK publishes some of the most detailed travel advice on Colombia. Its 30 October 2026 version advises against all but essential travel to Catatumbo, most of Arauca, the 5 km strip along the Venezuelan border, much of Chocó and the Pacific coast of Valle del Cauca, among other areas. Neither Boyacá nor Cundinamarca appears on those lists.

That is not the same as zero risk. The same advice notes that the most common problem for visitors is theft in large cities, including La Candelaria in Bogotá, and that mobile coverage is limited in the countryside. Check your own government's advice too: these documents change often.

twoBelts.heading: Is Muzo or Chivor dangerous? Two different histories
paragraphs: Search for "Colombia emeralds violence" and almost everything you find is about western Boyacá. There, between 1965 and 1990, the so-called green wars set emerald groups against each other for control of the mines, with thousands killed according to figures cited by the Colombian press. They ended with a peace accord signed on 12 July 1990. After 2013 there were new episodes of tension in that area.
Chivor lies in the other belt, the eastern one, about ten hours by road from Borbur. Its surroundings are shaped by mining and by two of the country's largest hydropower plants.

infrastructure.heading: The Chivor dam, the Guavio and the security forces
paragraphs: The reservoir you cross by ferry near Macanal is called La Esmeralda and feeds the Chivor plant: 1,000 MW and eight Pelton turbines, built between 1970 and 1977. To the south, at Mambita (Ubalá), the Guavio plant runs inside the mountain. At 1,260 MW it is the largest operating plant in Colombia, and a 2.2 km tunnel diverts the Chivor river into its reservoir.

Both are strategic infrastructure, and there is a permanent presence of Colombia's security forces in the region. We say this from our experience operating there, not as an official figure, and we do not publish locations or details of that presence. What we do: check local and mine conditions before every departure.

roads.heading: Roads, timing and rain
paragraphs: From Bogotá it takes about 5 to 6 hours. The last stretch is an unpaved mountain road, which is why the trip is planned in daylight, as the UK advice recommends for any rural road in the country.

The Colombian government has declared an El Niño event for 2026–2027 with a high probability of strong intensity, and unusual rainfall and landslides are expected. After heavy rain, ask about the road before setting out. The alternative route via Ubalá is only for motorbikes or 4x4s.

money.heading: Cash and signal
paragraphs: Bring cash for local expenses: there are no ATMs or card machines at the mines. If you need to withdraw money, do it in Bogotá, during banking hours, inside a bank or a shopping center.
Mobile signal in the countryside is patchy. The hacienda has WiFi. Before heading up to the mine, leave your itinerary with someone you trust.

photos.heading: What not to photograph
paragraphs: Photographing military installations or strategic state sites is illegal in Colombia. In practice: no photos of soldiers, checkpoints or the dam installations. Inside the mine, ask before photographing the miners. It is their workplace.

health.heading: Health and insurance
paragraphs: Chivor sits at about 2,000 m. That is not extreme altitude, but the humidity and the effort inside the mine are noticeable. Every tour includes medical assistance cover during the experience. Comprehensive travel insurance is not included, and if you are traveling from abroad we recommend it.
If you have a heart condition, a severe phobia or are recovering from an injury, message us before booking.

emergency.heading: In an emergency
paragraphs: Colombia's emergency number is 123. During the mining day the guide stays with the group from start to finish, and before the trip you get the team's WhatsApp for anything that comes up on the road.
One rule never changes: nobody enters the mine without a guide.

westernBoyaca.metaTitle: Fura and Tena, Muzo and Trapiche Emeralds | Andean Scapes
westernBoyaca.metaDescription: The Fura and Tena legend, the Muzo people who held off the Spanish for twenty years, trapiche emeralds and the road to the 1990 peace in western Boyacá.
westernBoyaca.title: Western Boyacá: Fura and Tena, Muzo and trapiche emeralds
westernBoyaca.lead: Fura and Tena is often called a Muisca legend. It is not. It belongs to the Muzo, a Carib-speaking people who raided their Muisca neighbors and kept the Spanish from founding a town in their land for twenty years.
westernBoyaca.imageAlt: Mountain landscape in the western Boyacá emerald region

muzos.heading: The Muzo, the emerald people
paragraphs: According to Colombia's register of geographic names, "muzo" comes from a Carib-family language and means "person". The Muzo mined emeralds by hand and used them as ornaments and for barter between clans.

Luis Lanchero went against them in 1539 and failed. Diego de Martínez tried in 1544, Melchor de Valdés in 1550 and Pedro de Ursúa in 1551. On 20 February 1559 Lanchero finally founded the town of Santísima Trinidad de los Muzos, and even then he had not fully subdued them.

legend.heading: The legend of Fura and Tena
paragraphs: In the version recorded by Julio Roberto Garavito, Are, the creator god, shaped Fura, the woman, and Tena, the man, from a handful of earth and threw them into the Minero river. He gave them eternal youth on one condition: they were to love only each other.

Then came Zarbi, a stranger searching for a flower that could cure every ill. Fura went with him to look for it, and in the forest they fell in love. With the betrayal came old age. Tena drove his war club into his own heart, lying across Fura's knees.

Zarbi was turned to stone, and his blood into the river that keeps the two lovers apart forever, now two hills. Fura's cries became butterflies; her tears, emeralds. That, the story says, is why the water of the Minero washes the emeralds of Muzo.

hills.heading: Where are Fura and Tena?
paragraphs: Fura and Tena are two hills facing each other across the Minero river, between San Pablo de Borbur, Pauna and Muzo. Published heights are about 840 m for Tena and 500 m for Fura. For the Muzo they were the seat of their gods.
The morpho butterfly, electric blue and black, is part of the area's culture. In the legend, every one of Fura's cries bursts into a flock of butterflies.

trapiche.heading: What is a trapiche emerald?
paragraphs: Some western emeralds show six dark arms radiating from the center, like the spokes of a sugar-cane mill wheel, a trapiche. Émile Bertrand first described them in 1879.

They come almost only from Muzo, Coscuez and Peñas Blancas. Older texts also credited Chivor, but a 2015 review in Gems & Gemology now considers that origin unlikely. If someone offers you a trapiche "from Chivor", ask twice.

furaStone.heading: An emerald named after the legend
paragraphs: In 1999 a Muzo mine produced a rough crystal of about 11,000 carats, more than two kilos. It was named Fura. According to press reports from 2011, a smaller one found with it was named Tena.

peace.heading: From conflict to the 1990 peace
paragraphs: The recent history of the west runs through the so-called green wars, three periods of violence between emerald groups from 1965 to 1990. The first alone, up to 1975, left more than 1,200 dead according to figures cited by the press. In 1980 Muzo had some 35,000 guaqueros, informal diggers.

On 12 July 1990 a peace accord closed that cycle; Muzo marked its 30th anniversary in 2020. After 2013 there were new episodes of tension. We tell this because it is part of the region and its people, not as an attraction.

visit.heading: What traveling west is like
paragraphs: Muzo sits at about 815 m and averages 26 °C, nothing like Chivor's 2,000 m and cold nights. From Chiquinquirá you reach it on Route 60 towards Pauna and Maripí.
Coscuez is in our catalog but has no dates right now. The experience available today is Chivor, in the eastern belt.
